title: Serve Robotics partners with Grubhub, becoming the shared robot layer for US food delivery
excerpt: Serve Robotics has added Grubhub, via a Wonder deal, to its Uber Eats and DoorDash tie-ups, and says it now has 2,000+ delivery robots on US streets.
content_html:
Serve Robotics, the sidewalk-delivery company that spun out of Uber, has added Grubhub to its roster of partners, a move that quietly turns it into something close to the neutral plumbing of America’s food-delivery robot business.

Through a deal with Wonder, Grubhub’s parent, Serve’s cooler-sized bots will start carrying takeaway orders placed on the Grubhub marketplace, beginning in Chicago, Los Angeles and Alexandria, Virginia.

It is the third of the big US delivery platforms to climb aboard. Serve already runs deliveries for Uber Eats, the app of its former parent, and for DoorDash, and by lining up all three it is wagering that the robots themselves, rather than any single app, are the asset worth owning.

That is a meaningfully different bet from the one most people picture when they imagine sharing the pavement with little delivery bots. The Grubhub rollout starts with more than 100 participating merchants in Chicago and close to 200 in Los Angeles.

Serve says it now has more than 2,000 robots deployed across the US, reaching around three million people and serving over 4,000 restaurants, a fleet it has built out aggressively since promising Uber Eats up to 2,000 bots back in 2023.

For a category long stuck in the perpetual-pilot phase, actually fielding thousands of working machines is the harder, less glamorous milestone.

Alongside the Grubhub deal, Serve said it had switched on two new markets with DoorDash, Washington, DC and San Jose, its seventh and eighth, lifting its combined reach to roughly eight million people across cities that also include Atlanta, Dallas and Miami.

It is experimenting, too, with “micro-depots”, small, low-cost bases meant to let it colonise fresh neighbourhoods without building out expensive full-scale facilities, exactly the sort of unglamorous logistics tweak that decides whether the economics ever close.

The company is no longer a pure sidewalk-delivery play. In 2026 it bought Diligent Robotics, maker of the Moxi hospital robot, and is now rolling out a faster Moxi 2.0 to hospitals in Chicago and Los Angeles, a bet that the same autonomy stack can shuttle medical supplies down a corridor as readily as a burrito down a street.

It has also launched an in-robot advertising line, complete with a hamburger-suited character called “Chomp” co-created with Grubhub, a reminder that a robot loitering on a busy pavement is also a moving billboard.

Delivery robots have been “about to arrive” for the better part of a decade, from Domino’s experiments with Nuro to Boston Dynamics teaching Spot to walk to the doorstep.

What has shifted is less the technology than the willingness of the big platforms to treat autonomy as a line item rather than a science project, and Serve’s pitch, to be the shared robot layer they all plug into, only pays off if that shift is real and durable.

The caveats are the familiar ones for a young, listed hardware company. Deploying robots is not the same as earning money from them; sidewalk delivery is a low-margin business with stubborn hardware, maintenance and mapping costs, and Serve, like its peers, is still spending to prove the unit economics rather than banking them.

The release, true to the genre, talks in robots and reach rather than revenue and margin. A milestone counted in bots on pavements is encouraging, but it is not yet one counted in profit.

Still, the direction is telling. By making itself the delivery robot that Uber Eats, DoorDash and now Grubhub can all summon, Serve is trying to become infrastructure, the dull but essential layer beneath the apps rather than a rival to them.

Whether America’s pavements can absorb thousands more little rolling coolers, and whether anyone can turn them into a durable profit, are the questions the next few thousand robots will have to answer.

content_html_zh:
从 Uber 中分离出来的人行道配送公司 Serve Robotics 已将 Grubhub 添加到其合作伙伴名单中，此举悄然将其转变为接近美国食品配送机器人业务的中立管道。

通过与 Grubhub 母公司 Wonder 达成的协议，Serve 的冷藏机器人将开始运送 Grubhub 市场上的外卖订单，从芝加哥、洛杉矶和弗吉尼亚州亚历山大开始。

它是美国第三个加入的大型配送平台。 Serve 已经为 Uber Eats（其前母公司的应用程序）和 DoorDash 提供送货服务，通过将这三个应用程序排列在一起，它押注机器人本身，而不是任何单个应用程序，才是值得拥有的资产。

这与大多数人想象的与小型送货机器人共享人行道时的想法截然不同。 Grubhub 的推出始于芝加哥的 100 多家参与商户和洛杉矶的近 200 家商户。

Serve 表示，目前在美国部署了 2,000 多台机器人，覆盖约 300 万人，为 4,000 多家餐厅提供服务，自 2023 年向 Uber Eats 承诺部署多达 2,000 台机器人以来，该公司一直在积极打造这一车队。

对于一个长期陷入永久试验阶段的类别来说，实际部署数千台工作机器是更困难、更不那么迷人的里程碑。

除了 Grubhub 交易之外，Serve 还表示，它已经与 DoorDash 合作开辟了两个新市场：华盛顿特区和圣何塞，这是第七和第八个市场，将其覆盖范围扩大到约 800 万人口，覆盖的城市还包括亚特兰大、达拉斯和迈阿密。

它还正在试验“微型仓库”，即小型、低成本的基地，旨在让它在不建造昂贵的全面设施的情况下殖民新的社区，这正是决定经济是否会关闭的那种乏味的物流调整。

该公司不再是一家纯粹的路边送货公司。 2026 年，它收购了 Moxi 医院机器人的制造商 Diligent Robotics，现在正在向芝加哥和洛杉矶的医院推出速度更快的 Moxi 2.0，赌注相同的自主堆栈可以像在街上运送卷饼一样轻松地在走廊上运送医疗用品。

它还推出了机器人内广告系列，其中包括与 Grubhub 共同创建的名为“Chomp”的汉堡包角色，提醒人们，在繁忙的人行道上徘徊的机器人也是一个移动的广告牌。

从 Domino 的 Nuro 实验到波士顿动力公司教 Spot 走到门口，送货机器人在过去十年的大部分时间里“即将到来”。

发生变化的与其说是技术，不如说是大平台愿意将自主视为一个项目，而不是一个科学项目，而Serve的宣传，即成为他们都插入的共享机器人层，只有在这种转变是真实且持久的情况下才会获得回报。

对于一家年轻的上市硬件公司来说，这些警告是很熟悉的。 部署机器人并不等同于通过机器人赚钱；人行道送货是一项低利润业务，硬件、维护和测绘成本很高，Serve 和同行一样，仍在花钱证明单位经济效益，而不是把它们存入银行。

该版本忠实于这一类型，谈论的是机器人和影响力，而不是收入和利润。 人行道上的机器人数量达到了令人鼓舞的里程碑，但尚未计入利润。

尽管如此，方向还是很能说明问题的。 通过将自己打造成 Uber Eats、DoorDash 和现在的 Grubhub 都可以召唤的送货机器人，Serve 试图成为基础设施，成为应用程序下面的乏味但重要的层，而不是它们的竞争对手。

美国的人行道能否容纳更多的小型滚动冷却器，以及是否有人可以将它们转化为持久的利润，是接下来的几千个机器人必须回答的问题。
